{"text": "the study combines two years of survey and behavioral data from American X/Twitter users, using a word embedding approach called the Super-Unsupervised (SU) method to measure online political hostility based on linguistic proximity to political and hostile language.", "page": 1}
{"text": "Our key measure of online political hostility is based on a word embeddings approach termed the Super-Unsupervised (SU) approach [60].", "page": 6}

{"text": "The SU approach was also validated against 2,469 hand-labeled posts rated by four expert raters using the definition of \"Political Hostility\" as: \"Degrading, harassing and intimidating online content grounded in political differences.\" [60]. The expert-coded set was approximately balanced across the two classes, so a naive baseline (always predicting the majority class) would achieve about 0.50 accuracy. We trained the score on a training split of these labelled posts and evaluated it on a held-out test split from the same domain (i.e., panelist posts), thereby avoiding in-sample inflation. Here, it reached 74% accuracy against a 50% baseline when dichotomized on a held-out test set.", "page": 7}

trace.claim: The SU method is validated through face validity, convergent and discriminant validity, criterion validity, external validity, and ecological validity, including a test with expert raters showing 74% accuracy in identifying political hostility.

{"text": "the present findings are mute on the exact causal relationships between the different indicators of political engagement and their antecedents. We interpret education and internal efficacy should be interpreted as distal antecedents of engagement rather than as direct causes of hostility. Political interest, political knowledge, and participation are more proximate to hostile political expression. An important caveat in this respect is that the analyses should not be taken to imply that, for example, more educated users are more hostile absent their generally higher levels of political engagement.", "page": 16}

{"text": "Fourth, although the primary measure of political hostility is supported by several validation exercises and robustness checks, no automated text-based measure perfectly captures the underlying construct. The measure may partly capture proximity to politically salient conflict language or hate-related political vocabulary rather than hostility alone. We therefore interpret the results in light of the validation evidence and robustness checks, while acknowledging this remaining construct-validity limitation.", "page": 16}

trace.claim: The primary measure of political hostility, while validated, may partly capture proximity to politically salient conflict language rather than hostility alone, and the study acknowledges this construct-validity limitation.
